warmup.q: A small reflection container that checks nothing in advance is asked for a MovingDay whose Driver needs the Truck, while the Truck needs the Driver. What happens?
options: It refuses with a clear message naming the loop
It waits forever, like a driver and a truck waiting for each other
A StackOverflowError, after about a thousand stack frames of the container calling itself
It builds a truck whose driver is null
warmup.why: The container builds each constructor argument first, so it asks for a truck, which asks for a driver, which asks for a truck, deeper each time, until the stack runs out. The demo's trace has 1,024 frames, as many as the JVM keeps. Waiting forever is tempting, because that's what people would do, but nothing in the code waits: it only goes deeper. Part 4's container named the loop because it had a check for it; the third section builds that check into the processor.

opening:
Picture seven o'clock on moving day. The truck is in the street and the packers are in the hall, but the driver has no route. Or the driver says he'll leave home when the truck picks him up, and the truck can't move without its driver. Or two printed routes lie on the table, and nobody knows which one was meant. Every one of these mistakes was on the plan the night before. Nobody read the plan closely enough to see it.

Last time, KSP wrote the plan during the build: a factory for each class and a component that builds the crew in order. The easy trap is to think that a plan which compiles is a plan that's right.

In this sitting we'll make three classic mistakes on purpose and meet each one on the day, in a reflection container. Then we'll catch all three the night before, each with its file, its line and its whole path. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at seven o'clock on moving day: a driver with no route, a driver waiting for the truck, and two routes on the table. On the street, the reflection container met them as a deep exception, a 1,024-frame stack overflow and a silent wrong turn. The night before, the processor names each one on its file and line, with its path.

In your own code, find a class that a framework builds and nothing calls directly. What would tell you, before the program starts, that its constructor can be satisfied?

Next, we'll measure what this buys at start-up, and let the slow GPS wait until it's needed. What does the generated plan save, in time and in classes?

sections.h: Three mistakes, met on the day: what a reflection container does with them
sections.html:
First, the words, since all of them are in play today. A dependency is an object another object needs, and dependency injection hands it in from outside, here through the constructor, which is constructor injection. A binding is one line of the plan: how to get one type. A singleton is built once per plan, and anything else is built new for each request. The graph is all the bindings, with an arrow for each "needs". Our KSP processor is a plug-in for the build that reads declarations and writes code. The component is the class it generates to build that graph, calling one generated factory, a small object that builds one class, for each.

Three mistakes in bindings are common enough to have names. A missing binding: somebody needs a type that nobody provides. A cycle: the "needs" arrows lead back to where they started. A duplicate binding: two bindings answer the same request, and the plan can't say which one is meant. Here they are, one small crew each:

Java
// missing: Driver forgot its @Inject
class Driver { Driver(Route route) { } }

// cycle: the driver waits for the truck, and the truck for the driver
class Driver { @Inject Driver(Route route, Truck truck) { } }
class Truck { @Inject Truck(Driver driver) { } }

// twice: two routes, and nothing says which one the driver means
@Module
public final class RouteModule {
    @Provides public Route highway() { return new Route("highway"); }
    @Provides public Route backRoads() { return new Route("back roads"); }
}
Kotlin
// missing: Driver forgot its @Inject
class Driver(val route: Route)

// cycle: the driver waits for the truck, and the truck for the driver
class Driver @Inject constructor(val route: Route, val truck: Truck)
class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver)

// twice: two routes, and nothing says which one the driver means
@Module
object RouteModule {
    @Provides fun highway(): Route = Route("highway")
    @Provides fun backRoads(): Route = Route("back roads")
}

Let's meet them the way a container that works things out on the street would. ReflectionContainer in this lesson's demos is about forty lines. It reads the sticky notes, the annotations, while the program runs. Ask it for a type, and it builds that type's constructor arguments first, then the type. It checks nothing in advance, on purpose. Asked for each crew's MovingDay, it printed:

--- missing: Driver has no @Inject
java.lang.IllegalStateException: no @Inject constructor on workbench.injector.l02.demo.missing.Driver
  19 stack frames, the first three:
    at workbench.injector.l02.demo.ReflectionContainer.construct(ReflectionContainer.kt:47)
    at workbench.injector.l02.demo.ReflectionContainer.get(ReflectionContainer.kt:37)
    at workbench.injector.l02.demo.ReflectionContainer.argumentsFor(ReflectionContainer.kt:52)
--- cycle: the driver waits for the truck
java.lang.StackOverflowError
  1024 stack frames, the first three:
    at java.base/java.lang.Class.privateGetDeclaredConstructors(Class.java:3540)
    at java.base/java.lang.Class.getConstructors(Class.java:2229)
    at workbench.injector.l02.demo.ReflectionContainer.construct(ReflectionContainer.kt:45)
--- twice: two routes, no names
no error: the driver takes the back roads

Three mistakes, three different failures, and every one of them at run time. The first names the class but not who asked for it, and its top frames are the container's own lines. The second is 1,024 frames of the container asking itself for a truck, which is as many frames as the JVM keeps in a stack trace by default. The third is the worst, because it isn't a failure at all. The container stored both routes under one key, and the second one it read quietly replaced the first. getDeclaredMethods() returns methods "not in any particular order", in the Javadoc's words, so which route wins is luck.

And lesson 1's processor? As promised, its walk has no memory of the path it is on, so it fails on the cycle the same way, only earlier. In a test compile it stopped with INTERNAL_ERROR, the exit code a test compile gives when a processor crashes, and a java.lang.StackOverflowError whose top frames are inside KotlinPoet. Earlier is better. But a stack overflow says nothing about which classes are to blame, at either time.

So the night-before check needs two things lesson 1's walk lacks: the path it's on, and the patience to report a problem and carry on.

sections.h: Nobody provides Driver: a missing binding named with its whole path
sections.html:
Lesson 1's message said Truck needs Driver, but nobody provides Driver. That's true, and it's enough when one class needs a driver. When ten classes do, you want to know how the plan got there. The walk already knows: it just has to keep the path it's on, the bindings it has entered and not yet left.

So lesson 2's walk carries a list called path. It adds a binding on the way in and removes it on the way out. When a dependency has no binding, the message is the path plus the missing type, joined with "needs". Here is the KSP walk next to the javac processor that does the same check:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: the javac processor in CompileTimeMistakesDemoJava
ExecutableElement constructor = ElementFilter.constructorsIn(cls.getEnclosedElements()).stream()
        .filter(c -> c.getAnnotation(Inject.class) != null).findFirst().orElse(null);
if (constructor == null) {                                       // nobody provides it
    List<String> needs = new ArrayList<>(path);
    needs.add(name);
    processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR,
            String.join(" needs ", needs) + ": nobody provides " + name, askedBy);
    return;
}
path.add(name);                                                  // on the way in
for (VariableElement p : constructor.getParameters()) walk(p.asType(), path, done, p);
path.remove(path.size() - 1);                                    // on the way out
done.add(name);
Kotlin
fun visit(binding: Binding) {
    path += binding                                              // on the way in
    for (dependency in binding.dependencies) {
        val target = bindingFor(dependency.key, dependency.type)
        when {
            target == null -> error(                             // nobody provides it
                (path + dependency.key).joinToString(" needs ") +
                    ": nobody provides ${dependency.key}. ${hint(dependency.key)}",
                dependency.node,                                 // the parameter that asks
            )
            target.key in done -> Unit                           // already built: shared
            // ... the cycle check comes here, in the next section
            else -> visit(target)
        }
    }
    path.removeAt(path.lastIndex)                                // on the way out
    done[binding.key] = binding
}

Two details make the message useful. The error goes on dependency.node, the parameter that asks, so logger.error prints that parameter's file and line. And the walk doesn't stop there. It reports, skips the missing piece and carries on, so one build can list every problem. The demo compiles the three broken crews from the last section, the very same files, in one build:

exit code: COMPILATION_ERROR
e: [ksp] Twice.kt:13: Route is provided twice: by RouteModule.highway() and by RouteModule.backRoads(). Give each one its own @Named qualifier and ask for the one you mean.
e: [ksp] Missing.kt:8: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver. Add @Inject to its constructor, or a @Provides function in a @Module.
e: [ksp] Cycle.kt:7: Dependency cycle: Truck needs Driver needs Truck. Nothing in a cycle can be built first: change one of these constructors.

Missing.kt:8 is the truck's constructor, where the driver is asked for. (KSP prints the absolute path; the demo shortens it to the file name.) The javac twin finds the first two mistakes the same way. It reports through the Messager, javac's channel for a processor's messages, and prints Missing.java:7: error: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver. Java has had annotation processors that javac runs since Java 6; KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do the same job for Kotlin code.

A good message says what is wrong, where, and how to fix it. In a graph, "where" has two halves. The file and line tell you which parameter asked, and the path tells you why the plan needed it at all. The hint at the end covers "how": add @Inject, or a @Provides function in a @Module, which the last section brings in.

A missing binding is reported where it's asked for, with the path that led there. Report it there, and keep walking.

The other two lines in that output come from checks we haven't built yet. The cycle comes first, because the path makes it almost free.

try.title: Catch all three mistakes in one build
steps: Run CompileTimeMistakesDemo. It reads the same three files from disk, compiles them in one build with lesson 2's reference processors, and prints every error.

Match each error to its run-time failure in the last Try it. Which mistake did the reflection container not report at all?

alt.title: CompileTimeMistakesDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.injector.l02.demo; import java.net.URI; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import javax.annotation.processing.AbstractProcessor; import javax.annotation.processing.RoundEnvironment; import javax.annotation.processing.SupportedAnnotationTypes; import javax.lang.model.SourceVersion; import javax.lang.model.element.Element; import javax.lang.model.element.ExecutableElement; import javax.lang.model.element.TypeElement; import javax.lang.model.element.VariableElement; import javax.lang.model.type.TypeMirror; import javax.lang.model.util.ElementFilter; import javax.tools.Diagnostic; import javax.tools.DiagnosticCollector; import javax.tools.JavaCompiler; import javax.tools.JavaFileObject; import javax.tools.SimpleJavaFileObject; import javax.tools.ToolProvider; import workbench.injector.annotations.Component; import workbench.injector.annotations.Inject; // The closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor that walks each @Component's graph and reports a // missing binding or a cycle with its path, on the exact parameter, through the Messager. (It does the first // two checks only; the duplicates need modules.) main() runs javac in memory on two broken Java plans. // ./gradlew :injector:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.l02.demo.CompileTimeMistakesDemoJava public class CompileTimeMistakesDemoJava { @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.injector.annotations.Component") public static class GraphCheckProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { @Override public SourceVersion getSupportedSourceVersion() { return SourceVersion.latestSupported(); } @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment round) { for (Element component : round.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Component.class)) { // 1. Find for (ExecutableElement entry : ElementFilter.methodsIn(component.getEnclosedElements())) { walk(entry.getReturnType(), new ArrayList<>(), new HashSet<>(), entry); } } return true; } /** Depth first, with the path the walk is on: the same walk as the KSP processor's creationOrder. */ private void walk(TypeMirror type, List<String> path, Set<String> done, Element askedBy) { TypeElement cls = (TypeElement) processingEnv.getTypeUtils().asElement(type); String name = cls.getSimpleName().toString(); if (done.contains(name)) return; if (path.contains(name)) { // 2. Check List<String> loop = new ArrayList<>(path.subList(path.indexOf(name), path.size())); loop.add(name); error("Dependency cycle: " + String.join(" needs ", loop), askedBy); return; } ExecutableElement constructor = ElementFilter.constructorsIn(cls.getEnclosedElements()).stream() .filter(c -> c.getAnnotation(Inject.class) != null).findFirst().orElse(null); if (constructor == null) { List<String> needs = new ArrayList<>(path); needs.add(name); error(String.join(" needs ", needs) + ": nobody provides " + name, askedBy); return; } path.add(name); for (VariableElement p : constructor.getParameters()) walk(p.asType(), path, done, p); // 3. Read path.remove(path.size() - 1); done.add(name); } private void error(String message, Element element) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, message, element); } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<JavaFileObject> sources = List.of( source("movemate/missing/Missing.java", """ package movemate.missing; import workbench.injector.annotations.*; class Route { @Inject Route() {} } class Driver { Driver(Route route) {} } // forgot @Inject class Truck { @Inject Truck(Driver driver) {} } class Crew { @Inject Crew(Truck truck) {} } class MovingDay { @Inject MovingDay(Crew crew) {} } @Component interface MissingPlan { MovingDay movingDay(); } """), source("movemate/cycle/Cycle.java", """ package movemate.cycle; import workbench.injector.annotations.*; class Route { @Inject Route() {} } class Driver { @Inject Driver(Route route, Truck truck) {} } // waits for the truck class Truck { @Inject Truck(Driver driver) {} } // which waits for the driver class Crew { @Inject Crew(Truck truck) {} } class MovingDay { @Inject MovingDay(Crew crew) {} } @Component interface CyclePlan { MovingDay movingDay(); } """)); JavaCompiler javac = ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler(); DiagnosticCollector<JavaFileObject> diagnostics = new DiagnosticCollector<>(); JavaCompiler.CompilationTask task = javac.getTask(null, null, diagnostics, List.of("-classpath", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "-proc:only"), null, sources); task.setProcessors(List.of(new GraphCheckProcessor())); System.out.println("javac succeeded: " + task.call()); for (Diagnostic<? extends JavaFileObject> d : diagnostics.getDiagnostics()) { String file = d.getSource().getName().substring(d.getSource().getName().lastIndexOf('/') + 1); System.out.println(file + ":" + d.getLineNumber() + ": " + d.getKind().toString().toLowerCase() + ": " + d.getMessage(null)); } } private static JavaFileObject source(String path, String text) { return new SimpleJavaFileObject(URI.create("string:///" + path), JavaFileObject.Kind.SOURCE) { @Override public CharSequence getCharContent(boolean ignoreEncodingErrors) { return text; } }; } }

The Java twin prints javac succeeded: false, Missing.java:7: error: ... and Cycle.java:6: error: Dependency cycle: Truck needs Driver needs Truck. sections.h: The driver waits for the truck: finding a cycle before anyone moves
sections.html:
A cycle is a path of "needs" arrows that comes back to where it started: the truck needs a driver, and the driver needs the truck. Nothing in a cycle can be built first, because each constructor needs the other object already built.

With the path in hand, finding one takes a single check. Before visiting a dependency, ask whether it's already on the path. If it is, the walk has come back to a binding it's still inside. The loop is the part of the path from that binding on, plus the binding once more:

Java
if (path.contains(name)) {                                       // we are inside it already
    List<String> loop = new ArrayList<>(path.subList(path.indexOf(name), path.size()));
    loop.add(name);
    processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR,
            "Dependency cycle: " + String.join(" needs ", loop), askedBy);
    return;
}
Kotlin
path.any { it.key == target.key } -> {                           // we are inside it already
    val loop = path.dropWhile { it.key != target.key } + target
    error(
        "Dependency cycle: ${loop.joinToString(" needs ")}. " +
            "Nothing in a cycle can be built first: change one of these constructors.",
        dependency.node,
    )
}

Let's trace the broken crew from the walk's point of view. It enters MovingDay, then Crew, then Truck, then Driver, so the path is [MovingDay, Crew, Truck, Driver]. The driver's first parameter, the route, is fine. His second asks for Truck, which is on the path. Drop everything before Truck, add Truck again, and the loop reads Truck needs Driver needs Truck. The error goes on the driver's truck parameter, the arrow that closes the loop, as the figure shows.

The order of the checks matters. A binding that is finished is shared, not a loop, even when two classes need it: the crew and the moving day both need a route. So the walk checks done before it checks the path. Part 4's container made the same choice for the same reason.

In the real build it looks like this. Uncomment val truck: Truck in app/src/l02/.../Driver.kt and run ./gradlew :injector:app:kspL02Kotlin:

e: [ksp] .../labs/injector/app/src/l02/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l02/Driver.kt:12: Dependency cycle: Truck needs Driver needs Truck. Nothing in a cycle can be built first: change one of these constructors.
> Task :injector:app:kspL02Kotlin FAILED

Here the picture breaks again. On a real street, the driver and the truck company would sort it out with a phone call. Code can't negotiate. Someone has to change a constructor, and the message lists the constructors to look at. Lesson 3 meets Lazy, which delays building something until it's first used, but our processor still calls a loop through a Lazy a cycle. It's the safe answer.

A cycle is a request for something you're still building. Check the path before you visit.

Missing bindings and cycles are about too few answers. The last mistake is one answer too many.

sections.h: Two routes: duplicate bindings, @Named, and a @Module for a class you can't annotate
sections.html:
So far every binding came from an @Inject constructor. That works for your own classes. But MoveMate's Route now comes from a maps library, and you can't put a sticky note on a class you can't edit. A module fills that gap: an object whose functions say how to get such things. Each function marked @Provides is a binding, and its parameters are its own dependencies:

Java
// The same module in Java: a Kotlin object compiles to a final class with one INSTANCE
@Module
public final class RouteModule {
    public static final RouteModule INSTANCE = new RouteModule();
    private RouteModule() { }

    @Provides @Singleton @Named("highway")
    public Route highway() { return new Route("highway", 42); }

    @Provides @Singleton @Named("back roads")
    public Route backRoads() { return new Route("back roads", 51); }
}
Kotlin
@Module
object RouteModule {
    @Provides @Singleton @Named("highway")
    fun highway(): Route = Route("highway", 42)

    @Provides @Singleton @Named("back roads")
    fun backRoads(): Route = Route("back roads", 51)
}

Take the names away first, as in the third broken crew, and the plan has two answers to one question. The reflection container shrugged and kept whichever one it read last. The processor's duplicate check groups every @Provides function by its key, the type plus any qualifier. Then it reports every binding after the first on its own line: Twice.kt:13: Route is provided twice: by RouteModule.highway() and by RouteModule.backRoads(). An @Inject constructor counts too. Provide a Route from a module while Route also has an @Inject constructor, and the message says by Route's @Inject constructor and by RouteModule.route().

The fix is a qualifier: a name that tells two bindings of the same type apart. @Named("highway") on a @Provides function marks one binding, and @Named("highway") on a parameter asks for exactly that one:

Java
public class Driver {
    @Inject
    public Driver(@Named("highway") Route route) { /* ... */ }
}

public class MovingDay {
    @Inject
    public MovingDay(Crew crew, @Named("back roads") Route familyRoute) { /* ... */ }
}
Kotlin
@Singleton
class Driver @Inject constructor(@Named("highway") val route: Route)

@Singleton
class MovingDay @Inject constructor(val crew: Crew, @Named("back roads") val familyRoute: Route)

Now the truck takes the highway, and the family follows in their own car on the back roads. The generated plan names each route after its qualifier, so the two never mix: private val highwayRoute: Route = RouteModule.highway(), private val backRoadsRoute: Route = RouteModule.backRoads(), and the driver's line reads DriverFactory.create(highwayRoute).

A qualifier is part of the key, so a misspelt one is simply a missing binding. Ask for @Named("hihgway"), a road no map has heard of, and the walk says so, path and all: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver needs @Named("hihgway") Route: nobody provides @Named("hihgway") Route.

Duplicates belong to the modules, not to one component, so the processor checks them once per build, before it walks any component. Then each component's walk adds what it finds. Missing, circular or doubled, every mistake gets its own line in one build, and a component is written only when its plan is clean. When a component isn't written, the app code that uses it can't compile either. So KSP adds follow-on lines such as MovingDayApp.kt:6: Unresolved reference 'GeneratedMovingDayComponent'. Fix the first errors; those go away with them.

That leaves the limit of today's checks. They see what the plan is made of: types, names and constructors. They can't tell you that a route of 42 minutes is a bad one, or that a constructor will throw on the day. Those stay run-time problems.

In RouteModule.kt, change @Named("back roads") to @Named("highway"). Predict every error, run ./gradlew :injector:app:kspL02Kotlin, then change it back.

compare.title: One mistake, two messengers: javac's Messager and KSP's logger

java.title: GraphCheckProcessor (javac)
java.html: // in the processor: the message, and the element it is about processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver", parameter); // what the demo's DiagnosticCollector gives back: the file, the line, the message // Missing.java:7: error: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver

kotlin.title: Graph (KSP)
kotlin.html: // in the processor: the message, and the symbol it is about logger.error( "MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver. " + hint(key), dependency.node, ) // what the build prints: the absolute path and the line, no column // e: [ksp] /.../Missing.kt:8: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver. ...

compare.note: Both APIs take a message and the symbol it is about, and both report the declaration's line, which for a parameter is the parameter's own line. A javac diagnostic also carries a column, and javac's default printer shows the source line with a caret; KSP prints e: [ksp], the absolute path and the line, with no column. In both, an error lets the current round finish, so a processor that reports and carries on gets every mistake into one build. The difference is in the model, not the messenger: our KSP processor reads Kotlin types such as Lazy<T> and nullability as Kotlin sees them, where javac sees the Java view of them.

Read Bindings.kt: a Key is a type plus an optional qualifier, and prints as Driver or @Named("highway") Route. A Binding is a ConstructorBinding or a ProvidesBinding; each has dependencies, a node for errors and an origin for messages. Read: write Graph.creationOrder with a path list. Add a binding on the way in and remove it on the way out. For each dependency, decide between missing, shared (already in done), cycle (on the path) and visit, and use error(...) and hint(key) for the messages.

Prove: run the tests until all eight pass. Then run ./gradlew :injector:app:kspL02Kotlin -Pmine=l02, uncomment val truck: Truck, in app/src/l02/.../Driver.kt, run it again and read your own cycle message. Comment the line out again.
From memory: without looking, write the four cases for one dependency (missing, shared, cycle, visit) with their two messages. Check them against your creationOrder.
hints: (path + dependency.key).joinToString(" needs ") works because a Binding prints as its key.
Check target.key in done before the path. A finished binding is shared, not a cycle, even when two classes need it.
path.dropWhile { it.key != target.key } + target gives the loop from the repeated binding: [Truck, Driver, Truck].
Report and carry on: don't leave the walk after an error. The test every problem is reported in one build counts exactly three errors.
For an entry point that nobody provides, the message starts with entry.name, for example MovingDayComponent.helicopter() needs Helicopter: nobody provides Helicopter.

drill.title: Write a cycle finder from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write findCycle(needs, start): needs maps each class name to the names its constructor asks for, and the function returns the first loop a depth-first walk from start meets, as [Truck, Driver, Truck], or null when there is none. A name the walk has finished is shared, not a loop. Then write it in Java.

answer.html: fun findCycle(needs: Map<String, List<String>>, start: String): List<String>? { val done = mutableSetOf<String>() val path = mutableListOf<String>() fun visit(name: String): List<String>? { if (name in done) return null // finished: shared, not a loop if (name in path) return path.dropWhile { it != name } + name // back where we started path += name // on the way in for (d in needs[name].orEmpty()) visit(d)?.let { return it } path.removeAt(path.lastIndex) // on the way out done += name return null } return visit(start) } // findCycle(mapOf("Truck" to listOf("Driver"), "Driver" to listOf("Truck")), "Truck") == [Truck, Driver, Truck]

alt.title: FindCycle.java
alt.html: static List<String> findCycle(Map<String, List<String>> needs, String start) { return visit(start, needs, new HashSet<>(), new ArrayList<>()); } static List<String> visit(String name, Map<String, List<String>> needs, Set<String> done, List<String> path) { if (done.contains(name)) return null; // finished: shared, not a loop if (path.contains(name)) { // back where we started List<String> loop = new ArrayList<>(path.subList(path.indexOf(name), path.size())); loop.add(name); return loop; } path.add(name); // on the way in for (String d : needs.getOrDefault(name, List.of())) { List<String> loop = visit(d, needs, done, path); if (loop != null) return loop; } path.remove(path.size() - 1); // on the way out done.add(name); return null; }

recap: A missing binding, a cycle and a duplicate binding are mistakes in the plan. A reflection container meets them only on the day: as an exception from its own code, as a 1,024-frame StackOverflowError, or as no error at all.
Keep the path the walk is on. A missing binding is reported on the parameter that asks, with the path joined by "needs"; a cycle is a dependency that is still on the path.
Check the finished set before the path: a finished binding is shared, not a loop.

A @Module object's @Provides functions bind types you can't annotate. A @Named qualifier is part of the key, so two bindings of one type need different names, and a misspelt name is a missing binding.
Report with logger.error(message, symbol) and carry on: one build lists every mistake, and the component is written only when its plan is clean.
The limit: the checks see types, names and constructors, not values. A constructor that throws on the day is still a run-time problem.

explain.prompt: Using the truck and the driver, explain why a cycle check needs the path the walk is on, and not just the set of bindings it has finished. Then say why the processor reports problems and carries on instead of stopping at the first.
explain.answer: The finished set only says what has been fully built. When the driver asks for the truck, the truck isn't finished yet: the walk entered it, went down into its constructor and is now inside the driver. So the finished set says nothing, and a walk with only that set goes round and round until the stack runs out, which is what lesson 1's processor did. The path is the list of bindings the walk has entered and not left: MovingDay, Crew, Truck, Driver. If the driver asks for something on that list, the walk has come back to something it's still building, so that's a loop, and the loop is the part from the truck on: Truck needs Driver needs Truck. The order of the checks matters: something in the finished set is shared, not a loop, so check it first. Reporting with logger.error and carrying on puts each mistake on its own file and line, and the round still finishes, so one build tells you about the missing driver, the loop and the two routes together, instead of one per build.

deeper.html:
When the component isn't written, every line of your code that uses it breaks too, and KSP adds follow-on messages after the real ones, with the file name only: e: [ksp] MovingDayApp.kt:6: Unresolved reference 'GeneratedMovingDayComponent'. They come from a type check KSP runs on a failed build, and they disappear when the first errors are fixed. Read the messages from the top.

Where an error points is a choice the processor makes. Ours puts a missing binding on the parameter that asks, a cycle on the parameter that closes the loop, and a duplicate on the second binding. Each is the line you would edit. javac's Messager has overloads that take an AnnotationMirror or an AnnotationValue too, so a Java processor can point at a single annotation argument, such as a misspelt @Named value. KSP's logger takes any KSNode, and its location is the line of the declaration.

The checks are cheap because the graph is small and each binding is visited once. Resolving types is the expensive part of KSP, and the walk resolves each parameter's type once per binding. A much larger graph would want each resolved type cached in the binding, which ours does with by lazy.

Our checks stop at what the plan is made of. They don't warn about a binding nobody uses, or a singleton that depends on something built fresh each time and so keeps one copy for good. Real tools add checks like those; once you have the graph and the path, each one is a few lines in the same walk.
